Per-metric state for the calendar price windows: metric -> {state, cause, reason, observed}. Sparse -- an entry exists only for a metric whose state is not APPLICABLE, so a populated numeric column must never sit beside an entry, and a NULL numeric column with no entry is a contract violation rather than a default. NULL (not '{}') means the row was never assessed: written before FACTOR_MODEL_V3 or by a producer that does not assess. Same vocabulary as screener.universe.metric_states.

business_rule: Membership comes from screener.universe.is_asx200 / is_asx300, set by compute/engine/asx_indices.py -- a job whose own freshness is listed as NOT INDEPENDENTLY OBSERVABLE in the output-freshness registry, because it writes no timestamp. transformation_rule: constituents matching the filter
business_rule: ACTIVE constituents only. Will not equal 200 or 300: the flag is whatever asx_indices last wrote, and delisted or suspended members are excluded by status.

transformation_rule: strictly positive one-week return
business_rule: gainers + losers + unchanged CAN BE LESS THAN stock_count, because a constituent with a NULL return_1w falls in none of the three. That shortfall is the honest representation of unknown -- see `unchanged`.

transformation_rule: strictly negative one-week return
STRICTLY FLAT - exactly zero
business_rule:
NULL IS DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED. The filter previously read `return_1w = 0 OR return_1w IS NULL`, which reported a company whose return we do not have as a company whose price did not move. Once summed into one integer the page cannot tell them apart.
The run now REFUSES rather than folding unknowns in: a separate `no_return` count is computed, and if it is non-zero the job raises SnapshotIncomplete, because this table has no column to record it. The stated fix when that fires is a no_return column, not a wider FILTER.

transformation_rule: mean one-week return across constituents
business_rule: EQUAL-WEIGHTED, not capitalisation-weighted, so it is not the index's own return and will diverge from the published ASX200 move. SQL AVG ignores NULLs, so the denominator is constituents WITH a return, not stock_count.

transformation_rule: summed constituent market cap, divided by 1000
business_rule:
UNIT UNCONFIRMED -- see the header note and OPEN_FINDINGS.md. The divisor yields billions only if screener.universe.market_cap is in MILLIONS; that column is populated from market.valuation_snapshot.market_cap, which carries EODHD's raw full-currency figure. On a raw-AUD basis this column holds thousands of AUD under a name that says billions.
SUM also ignores NULLs, so a constituent with no market cap silently lowers the total rather than making it NULL.

transformation_rule: column default now() on insert, NOW() on upsert
business_rule: LOAD TIME, not event time. A backfill run writes an old snapshot_date with today's created_at, and that is correct: the pair records both what the row is about and when it was produced.

transformation_rule: the date the snapshot describes
business_rule: EVENT TIME. Note it is NOT constrained to match the period_metrics row the high/low came from -- that join takes MAX(computed_date) independently, deliberately, "to avoid a CURRENT_DATE race when the nightly jobs run in different orders". So period_high and period_low on a given row can come from a different date than snapshot_date, and nothing on the row records which.

valid_values: GAINER_1W, GAINER_1M, GAINER_3M, LOSER_1W, LOSER_1M, LOSER_3M, GAINER, LOSER (legacy aliases of the 1W panels), ACTIVE, BUYING, SELLING. GAINER_1D and LOSER_1D are DECLARED BUT NEVER WRITTEN.
transformation_rule: panel identifier
business_rule:
The 1D PANELS DO NOT EXIST. RETURN_PERIODS declares ("1D", "return_1d"), but screener.universe has never had a return_1d column. Availability is now established before any statement runs, so the panel is skipped with a log line instead of raising -- and the entry is kept in the declaration on purpose, because deleting it would hide the real gap: a one-day return is not computed anywhere.
GAINER and LOSER are aliases assigned in Python from the 1W panels for backwards compatibility, so those rows are DUPLICATES of GAINER_1W and LOSER_1W under a second name.
derivation_formula: f'{GAINER|LOSER}_{1D|1W|1M|3M}', plus GAINER, LOSER, ACTIVE, BUYING, SELLING

transformation_rule: 1-based position within the panel
business_rule: Rank is assigned by the ORDER BY of each panel, which differs: the gainer and loser panels order by the period return, ACTIVE by raw volume, BUYING and SELLING by volume / avg_volume_20d. Rank 1 means something different in each.

transformation_rule: the period return for THIS PANEL, whichever period that is
business_rule:
THE COLUMN NAME IS WRONG FOR MOST ROWS. A GAINER_3M row carries the THREE-MONTH return in a column called return_1w; a GAINER_1M row carries the one-month return there. Only the 1W panels (and their GAINER / LOSER aliases) hold an actual one-week return.
The transform is explicit about it -- "stored in the return_1w column for query consistency" -- so a consumer must read snapshot_type to know what unit of time this number spans. Any query that aggregates return_1w across snapshot_types is mixing periods.
derivation_formula: period_return = u.<RETURN_PERIODS[snapshot_type]> ; stored into the return_1w column
